fields.label: Surface Parcel
fields.help: (not editable here) A short, unique name you provided the parcel when creating it in the map utility on the Parcels Page.

fields.label: Land Use
fields.help: (not editable here) The parcel's dominant land use that you provided when creating it in the map utility on the Parcels Page.

fields.label: Area
fields.help: (auto-calculated) Surface area of the parcel (square kilometers)

fields.label: R
fields.help: Enter the rainfall erosivity index of the Universal Soil Loss Equation (100 foot-tons per acre). Valid values are >= 0. The index reflects the ability of rainfall (especially intense rainfall or large amounts of rainfall over a longer period of time) to detach and transport soil. The default value of 300 is at the high end of recommended default values from U.S. EPA 2005 (Human Health Risk Assessment Protocol for Hazardous Waste Combustion Facilities); their default values are 50 to 300, see Table B-4-13. It is a relatively high value for most U.S. locations and is representative of locations near the southeastern U.S. but away from the Gulf Coast (see Figure 1 of Wischmeier and Smith 1978 [Predicting rainfall erosion losses. A guide to conservation planning]). Selecting the Get USDA Soil Data button will obtain a site-specific estimate for you. See the TRIM User Guide Appendix for full reference information.

fields.label: K
fields.help: Enter the erodibility index of the Universal Soil Loss Equation (tons per acre per [100 foot-tons per acre]). Valid values are >= 0. The index is the rate of soil loss normalized to the rainfall erosivity index as measured on a standardized unit plot. The default value of 0.36 is close to the 0.39 value recommended by U.S. EPA 2005 (Human Health Risk Assessment Protocol for Hazardous Waste Combustion Facilities; see Table B-4-13) and is based on U.S. EPA 1994 (Draft Guidance for Performing Screening Level Risk Analyses at Combustion Facilities Burning Hazardous Wastes. Attachment C, Draft Exposure Assessment Guidance for RCRA Hazardous Waste Combustion Facilities). Selecting the Get USDA Soil Data button will obtain a site-specific estimate for you. See the TRIM User Guide Appendix for full reference information.

fields.label: S
fields.help: Enter the slope gradient of the Universal Soil Loss Equation (percent). Valid values are >= 0. The gradient is the ratio of soil loss from the field slope gradient to that from a 9% slope under the same conditions. S, along with the slope length (L), can be used to calculate the topographical length-slope factor (LS): (0.065 + 0.0456S + 0.006541S2)*(L/72.5)Y, where Y = 0.2 if S < 1, 0.3 if 1 ≤ S < 3, 0.4 if 3 ≤ S < 5, and 0.5 if S ≥ 5 (http://www.omafra.gov.on.ca/english/engineer/facts/12-051.htm#t3a). In this editable table, you may directly enter the LS value (in this case, you will not enter the values of S and L), or you may enter the values of S and L and then the LS value will be calculated for you. Selecting the Get USDA Soil Data button will obtain a site-specific estimate of S for you.

fields.label: L
fields.help: Enter the slope length of the Universal Soil Loss Equation (feet). Valid values are >= 0. The length is the ratio of soil loss from the field slope length to that from a 72.5-foot length under the same conditions. L, along with the slope gradient (S), can be used to calculate the topographical length-slope factor (LS): (0.065 + 0.0456S + 0.006541S2)*(L/72.5)Y, where Y = 0.2 if S < 1, 0.3 if 1 ≤ S < 3, 0.4 if 3 ≤ S < 5, and 0.5 if S ≥ 5 (http://www.omafra.gov.on.ca/english/engineer/facts/12-051.htm#t3a). In this editable table, you may directly enter the LS value (in this case, you will not enter the values of S and L), or you may enter the values of S and L and then the LS value will be calculated for you. Selecting the Get USDA Soil Data button will obtain a site-specific estimate of L for you.

fields.label: LS
fields.help: Enter the topographical length-slope factor of the Universal Soil Loss Equation (unitless). Valid values are >= 0. The factor is the expected ratio of soil loss from the field slope to that measured on a standardized unit plot. The default value of 1.5 is a recommended default in U.S. EPA 2005 (Human Health Risk Assessment Protocol for Hazardous Waste Combustion Facilities; see Table B-4-13) and is based on U.S. EPA 1994 (Draft Guidance for Performing Screening Level Risk Analyses at Combustion Facilities Burning Hazardous Wastes. Attachment C, Draft Exposure Assessment Guidance for RCRA Hazardous Waste Combustion Facilities). Selecting the Get USDA Soil Data button will obtain site-specific estimates of the S and L values, which then will be used to calculate LS as: (0.065 + 0.0456S + 0.006541S2)*(L/72.5)Y, where Y = 0.2 if S < 1, 0.3 if 1 ≤ S < 3, 0.4 if 3 ≤ S < 5, and 0.5 if S ≥ 5 (http://www.omafra.gov.on.ca/english/engineer/facts/12-051.htm#t3a). See the TRIM User Guide Appendix for full reference information.

fields.label: C
fields.help: Enter the cover/management factor of the Universal Soil Loss Equation (unitless). Valid values are >= 0. This factor is the expected ratio of soil loss under certain cover and management conditions to that of a field under clean-tilled continuous fallow. The default value of 0.5 for agricultural parcels is within the range of 0.1 to 0.7 discussed in U.S. EPA 2005 (Human Health Risk Assessment Protocol for Hazardous Waste Combustion Facilities [HHRAP]; see Table B-4-13); this includes parcels that are modeled as tilled soil-only parcels but are destined to be evaluated for gardening/crop farming in the farmer or gardener exposure scenarios. The default value of 1 for bare-soil parcels not destined to be evaluated for farmer/gardener exposures is recommended by U.S. EPA 1998 (Methodology for assessing health risks associated with multiple pathways of exposure to combustor emissions; see Section 7.2.7). The default value of 0.1 for all other parcels (forested, grasses/herbs, and untilled soil-only parcels destined to be evaluated for livestock exposures in the farmer exposure scenario) is that recommended by HHRAP and U.S. EPA 1994 (Draft Guidance for Performing Screening Level Risk Analyses at Combustion Facilities Burning Hazardous Wastes. Attachment C, Draft Exposure Assessment Guidance for RCRA Hazardous Waste Combustion Facilities). See the TRIM User Guide Appendix for full reference information.

fields.label: P
fields.help: Enter the supporting practices factor of the Universal Soil Loss Equation (unitless). Valid values are >= 0. This factor is the expected ratio of soil loss under specific soil-conservation practices like contouring and terracing to that of a field with up- and down-slope tillage. The default value of 1 assumes the absence of these conservation practices.

fields.label: A
fields.help: Enter the unit soil loss of the parcel (kilograms per square meter per day). Valid values are >= 0.

fields.label: a
fields.tooltip: sediment delivery ratio: empirical intercept coefficient (unitless)
fields.help: Enter the empirical intercept coefficient of the sediment delivery ratio (unitless). Valid values are >= 0. The ratio is the fraction of gross erosion from a specific area that is delivered to another area, and it is defined as a*Area<sup>-b</sup> (area in square meters). In this editable table, you may directly enter the ratio value (in this case, you will not enter the values of coefficients a or b), or you may enter the values of a and b and then the ratio value will be calculated for you. The default intercept values depend on the parcel area and are from Vanoni 1975 (Sedimentation Engineering) as cited by Section 7.2.7 of U.S. EPA 1998 (Methodology for assessing health risks associated with multiple pathways of exposure to combustor emissions) and Table B-4-14 of U.S. EPA 2005 (Human Health Risk Assessment Protocol for Hazardous Waste Combustion Facilities): 2.1 for parcel areas ≤ 0.1 square miles, 1.9 for parcel areas > 0.1 to ≤ 1.0 square miles, 1.4 for parcel areas > 1.0 to ≤ 10 square miles, 1.2 for parcel areas > 10 to ≤ 100 square miles, and 0.6 for parcel areas > 100 square miles. See the TRIM User Guide Appendix for full reference information.

fields.label: b
fields.tooltip: sediment delivery ratio: empirical slope coefficient (unitless)
fields.help: Enter the empirical slope coefficient of the sediment delivery ratio (unitless). Valid values are >= 0. The ratio is the fraction of gross erosion from a specific area that is delivered to another area, and is defined as a*Area<sup>-b</sup> (area in square meters). In this editable table, you may directly enter the ratio value (in this case, you will not enter the values of coefficients a or b), or you may enter the values of a and b and then the ratio value will be calculated for you. The default slope value is 0.125 from Vanoni 1975 (Sedimentation Engineering) as cited by Section 7.2.7 of U.S. EPA 1998 (Methodology for assessing health risks associated with multiple pathways of exposure to combustor emissions) and Table B-4-14 of U.S. EPA 2005 (Human Health Risk Assessment Protocol for Hazardous Waste Combustion Facilities). See the TRIM User Guide Appendix for full reference information.

fields.label: SD
fields.help: Enter the sediment delivery ratio (unitless). Valid values are >= 0. The ratio is the fraction of gross erosion from a specific area that is delivered to another area, and is defined as a*Area<sup>-b</sup> (area in square meters; these parameters also are in this editable table, with Area being auto-calculated). In this editable table, you may directly enter the ratio value (in this case, you will not enter the values of coefficients a or b), or you may enter the values of a and b and then the ratio value will be calculated for you.

fields.label: Total Effective Erosion Rate
fields.help: Enter the total effective erosion rate of the parcel (kilograms per square meter per day). Valid values are >= 0. Under Options 2 and 3 on this page, it is calculated as: unit soil loss (A) * sediment delivery ratio (SD) (and * organic enrichment ratio for organic contaminants). A can be calculated using the Universal Soil Loss Equation as: rainfall erosivity index (R) * soil erodibility index (K) * topographical length-slope factor (LS) * cover/management factor (C) * supporting practices factor (P), with additional unit conversions to go from tons per acre per year to kilograms per square meter per day. SD can be calculated as: empirical intercept factor (a) * area<sup>-empirical slope factor (b)</sup> (area in square meters).
